# Current law — tracker-workflow

Governance snapshot `bf23395ed1e05940`. 20 rule(s) in force.

This file carries CURRENT law for this domain and nothing else. Superseded

## RULING 29 — three priority levels, ranked inside a section and never across sections

*`R-0029` · ACTIVE · author_confirmed · 2026-08-20 · also cited as `RULING 29`, `R29`, `R-29`*

**Not law. Recorded here.** Supersedes the P0/P1/P2/P3 scale and Prompt D's
definition of P0 ("blocks a reader-visible outcome before polling day"), which
is retired with the level it defined.

- **P1** — broken or blocking. Something a reader hits is wrong, or work cannot
  proceed until this is resolved. If it sits, the section stops.
- **P2** — needed for this section to be done. Not blocking today, but the
  section is not finished without it.
- **P3** — wanted, not needed. Real work, worth keeping, no consequence to
  deferring indefinitely.

The test is answerable without judgement: does something break or stall if this
waits? P1. Is the section done without it? If no, P2. If yes, P3.

**Priority is ranked independently inside each section.** P1 in one section has
no relationship to P1 in another, and the two are never compared.

**The interpretation call this session had to make**, recorded so it is not
re-derived: RULING 31 gives *Needs Sean* its own three definitions, and all
three are about LOOKING AT THE PRODUCT — "it doesn't open", "confirm it reads
right", "tell me if you like it". That section also holds legal and business
decisions, which fit none of the three. So the general test above governs a
decision row in that section (does something break or stall if this waits?) and
RULING 31's definitions govern a review row. `B05` (find counsel) is P1 under
that reading because two other rows cannot start until it closes; `B02`
(trademark search) is P3 because nothing waits on it. If the author wants a
single scale there, one sentence settles it.

## RULING 30 — five P1 rows maximum per section, and an over-cap section is STOPPED

*`R-0030` · ACTIVE · author_confirmed · 2026-08-20 · also cited as `RULING 30`, `R30`, `R-30`*

**Not law. Recorded here.** If a section exceeds five P1 rows, that is REPORTED
as a fact — the section is stopped — and nothing is relabelled to fit. **The cap
is never satisfied by demotion**, because a demotion changes the label and not
the situation.

Measured at this session's close: no section is over the cap. The highest is
Needs Sean at three.

## RULING 32 — every row has a home

*`R-0032` · ACTIVE · author_confirmed · 2026-08-20 · also cited as `RULING 32`, `R32`, `R-32`*

**Not law. Recorded here.** No holding section, no miscellaneous section, no
unsorted bucket. A row that fits nowhere is evidence the section list is
incomplete, and the answer is a named section proposed in the report — never a
junk drawer. `tests/tracker-stores.test.ts` fails the build on a row whose
section is not in `docs/tracker-sections.json`, and on the section list growing
one called `misc`, `other`, `unsorted`, `holding` or `general`.

## RULING 33 — gaps are not tracker rows

*`R-0033` · ACTIVE · author_confirmed · 2026-08-20 · also cited as `RULING 33`, `R33`, `R-33`*

**Not law. Recorded here.** A gap is a MEASUREMENT of coverage, not a task, and
it changes every time a hunt runs. Gaps live in the gap ledger, which is
generated and therefore current by construction. **The tracker holds the
decision to hunt Newbury; the ledger holds which of Newbury's bodies are still
dark.**

Audited at this session's close: **0 of 141 open rows is a bare gap.** Every row
that states a coverage number — `PB02`, `PB06`, `HUNT05`, `F03`, `D69` — also
states a decision to go and close it, which is what makes it a task. Five rows
carried a drifting COUNT in their title, which is a measurement wearing a task's
clothes; their titles now name the decision and the count stays in the row where
it belongs.

## RULING 35 — every section is a queue that empties

*`R-0035` · ACTIVE · author_confirmed · 2026-08-20 · also cited as `RULING 35`, `R35`, `R-35`*

**Not law. Recorded here.** Supersedes the single-file tracker
(`docs/tracker.csv`), which is frozen in place as the pre-rebuild snapshot.

The tracker is a WORKFLOW, not an ongoing list. A finished row leaves the
working view and lands in the resolved store. The working view shows only what
is left. **Nothing is ever deleted**; the resolved store is permanent and is the
record of what was decided and when.

Why it was needed, stated so the shape is recognisable if it recurs: the tracker
held 456 rows, 315 of them finished, in one view. The number the author looked
at was 456 rather than the 141 that were actually left.

## RULING 37 — who may move a row

*`R-0037` · AMENDED · author_confirmed · 2026-08-20 · also cited as `RULING 37`, `R37`, `R-37`*

**LAW.** Written into `CLAUDE.md` in the same commit, under the tracker rules.

- A session marks its own completed work Resolved and moves it, in every section
  except *Needs Sean*.
- **Only the author closes a Needs Sean row.** A session may never mark one
  Resolved or Conditionally resolved, and may never move one out, however
  obviously finished it appears.
- **Sessions OPEN Needs Sean rows.** Routing something to his attention is the
  session's job — he does not have to notice that something needs him.
- A guard test enforces both directions and fails the build if a session moves a
  Needs Sean row (`tests/tracker-stores.test.ts`).

## RULING 38 — the author's resolution notes are instructions, not commentary

*`R-0038` · ACTIVE · author_confirmed · 2026-08-20 · also cited as `RULING 38`, `R38`, `R-38`*

**LAW.** Written into `CLAUDE.md` in the same commit.

Every session opens by reading the resolved store for rows resolved since it
last ran and surfacing his notes (`corepack pnpm tracker:open`). A conditionally
resolved row's condition is a LIVE REQUIREMENT on that session — satisfied, or
reported as unsatisfied with the reason. The report states what was read and
what was done about each note. **A note read and ignored is a session failure.**

## RULING 41 — the author writes rows too

*`R-0041` · ACTIVE · author_confirmed · 2026-08-20 · also cited as `RULING 41`, `R41`, `R-41`*

**LAW.** Written into `CLAUDE.md` in the same commit.

Rows do not originate only from sessions. He adds rows by hand as he works
through the product, most often into *Visual feedback* and *Product / UI*.

- He types a description into the working store. **He does not invent an id** —
  the script assigns one in the correct format on its next run and reports which
  ids it assigned.
- Attribution records `Sean` as opening author. A row he wrote is fully
  attributed, never `UNKNOWN`.
- Every session reads his open rows at session start, alongside the RULING 38
  notes, so a row added on Monday reaches the next run without a prompt
  mentioning it. The session reports what it read.
- **A session may not reword, retitle, or delete one.** It may work the row, set
  a priority if none is set, and resolve it under RULING 37. The description is
  his. A guard test enforces this.

## RULING 43 — a source may not report success with zero normalized rows from a non-zero fetch

*`R-0043` · ACTIVE · author_confirmed · 2026-08-20 · also cited as `RULING 43`, `R43`, `R-43`*


*Adopted 2026-08-20 (NH Hunt brief, item 1). Supersedes nothing; it makes an
existing `CLAUDE.md` rule structural.*

This is the SIXTH sighting of the zero-row shape and the first to reach a
reader. `ical` reported `ok: true, fetched: 3, normalized: 0` with every drop
counter at zero on the 02:00Z refresh, carry-forward therefore did not run, and
Wilmot, New Hampshire went from 23 meetings to none on the page at 03255. The
feed was healthy when checked by hand minutes later.

Five written prohibitions did not stop it, because a written prohibition is
something a session has to remember at the moment it writes a `return`. **The
contract itself must refuse to express it.** `ReportingMeetingSource.normalizeWithDrops`
now returns an `Accounted<...>` — a branded type whose only constructor,
`accountedNormalize()` in `lib/sources/normalize-account.ts`, throws rather than
returning a value for the forbidden shape. A plain object literal no longer
compiles, and the composite routes the throw to `JOB`, which turns the run red.
A seventh instance fails at build, not on the site.

The invariant is deliberately narrow — documents in hand, nothing out, nothing
dropped — and NOT full input/output accounting, which is false of honest
adapters: one `.ics` document is twenty meetings.

## RULING 79 — a ruling closes the Needs Sean row it answers

*`R-0079` · ACTIVE · author_confirmed · 2026-08-22 · also cited as `RULING 79`, `R79`, `R-79`*

- **amends** → `R-0037`
  - what changed: where a dated ruling demonstrably answers a Needs Sean row, the session marks it Resolved and records the ruling number and shipping SHA
  - what survives, in force: RULING 37's rule that only the author closes a Needs Sean row stands for every row awaiting his judgement, and sessions still OPEN rows
- **sets** `tracker.needs_sean_closure` = `author-or-answering-ruling`


*Adopted 2026-08-22 (NJ Hunt 4, the session brief). **LAW** — written into
`CLAUDE.md` in the same session. **Amends RULING 37**, narrowly and
deliberately.*

RULING 37 says only the author closes a Needs Sean row. That stands for rows
awaiting his judgement. What it did not anticipate is the row he has ALREADY
ANSWERED: he rules in conversation, the ruling is recorded here and shipped, and
the row that asked the question sits open waiting for him to say the same thing
a second time in a spreadsheet. Needs Sean stood at 54 open and an unknown share
of those were already answered — the accumulation the section was built to
prevent.

- Where a dated ruling in this file **demonstrably** answers a Needs Sean row,
  the session marks it Resolved, records the ruling number and the shipping SHA
  on the row, and moves it.
- **Every such close is reported individually** with its ruling and SHA, so he
  can reverse any the session got wrong.
- Where no ruling answers the row, **it stays open and is named individually**.
  Ambiguity is not a licence to close.
- Rows that are genuinely his judgement and carry no ruling — a naming decision,
  a business call, a visual preference — stay open regardless of how long they
  have been there.

RULING 37's second half is untouched: **sessions still OPEN Needs Sean rows**,
and routing something to his attention remains the session's job.

## RULING 111 — a join is never a lookup for a fact that lives on only one side

*`R-0111` · ACTIVE · author_confirmed · 2026-08-23 · also cited as `RULING 111`, `R111`, `R-111`*


*Adopted 2026-08-23 (the questionnaire-and-corpora session, item 5). Law:
`CLAUDE.md`, **Data model conventions**. Supersedes nothing.*

**Before you ask a joined-up file a question, say which of the two files
actually holds the answer — and whether joining them can lose rows. If it can,
ask the file that holds the answer.**

A join puts two lists side by side by matching them on something. When the match
fails, the row does not come back at all — and a row that does not come back
looks exactly like a row where the answer was genuinely "nothing". **Those are
two completely different things and nothing in the output tells them apart.**

That is what happened here. The school-district classifier asked the
Census–NCES crosswalk whether a district is independent or run by another
government. **Only the Census file knows that.** NCES does not carry it. So the
question could have been asked of the Census file directly, and instead it was
asked of the two files stapled together — and the crosswalk's own report says,
in as many words, that **4,083 of 13,859 Census school systems have no NCES
match and are absent from it entirely.** Every one of those disappeared
silently, and the disappearance looked identical to a real answer of "we do not
know".

The reason the two files cannot be matched cleanly is worth stating, because it
is not a bug anyone can fix: **the two files share no identifier at all.** The
join is on state code plus a normalised district name, one-to-one, and a name
that matches more than one row on either side is thrown out rather than guessed
at. That is the correct way to do it and it still loses nearly three in ten.

So:

- **Say which side holds the fact, before querying.**
- **Say whether the join can drop rows.** A join on names always can.
- **If it can, query the side that holds the fact.**

*Why this is a ruling and not just a fixed bug.* Every instrument in this
project asks whether something came back. A dropped join row comes back as
nothing, and nothing is the same shape as an honest absence — so no existing
guard could ever have caught it. It is RULING 100's failure moved from reading a
document to reading a database: **a result that adds up is not a result that is
correct.**

---

The fuller one is above; this is the other, kept whole rather than merged, because merging

(Adopted 2026-08-23, item 5. It is **RULING 100's failure moved from reading a
document to reading a database**: that ruling catches an extraction that came
back with SOME of a document and reported all of it; this catches a query that
came back with some of a table and reported all of it.)

**Before querying a joined source, state which SIDE holds the fact and whether
the join can DROP ROWS. Where it can, query the side that holds it.**

*The rationale stays attached, because a stripped rule reads as guidance.* A
join drops the rows that fail to match, and **a dropped row is returned as
nothing — which is the same shape as a genuine absence.** No instrument in this
repo can tell those apart, because every instrument asks whether something came
back.

The district classifier asked the Census–NCES crosswalk whether a school system
is INDEPENDENT or DEPENDENT. **Only the Census file carries that fact**; NCES
does not. So a question one file could answer completely was put to two files
stapled together, and the crosswalk's own report states the cost outright:
**4,083 of 13,859 Census school systems have no NCES match and are absent from
it entirely** — 3,373 of 12,546 independent districts and 710 of 1,313
dependent ones. Every one of those vanished silently and read exactly like an
honest `UNCLASSIFIED`.

**The join was not built badly, and that is the point.** The two files share no
identifier at all: NCES publishes a Census ID only on the F-33 fiscal survey,
which is a separate acquisition. The crosswalk therefore matches on state code
plus normalised name, one-to-one, and counts an ambiguous name as UNMATCHED
rather than resolving it. That is the correct method and it still loses 29.46%.
**A correctly-built join that drops three rows in ten is not a lookup table**,
and no amount of improving it makes it one.

- **Which side holds the fact is stated before the query**, not discovered
  afterwards.
- **Whether the join can drop rows is stated.** A join on names always can.
- **Where it can, the query goes to the side that holds the fact.**

</details>

## RULING 115 — a drill is not a failure, and an alarm that cannot tell them apart spends the next real one

*`R-0115` · ACTIVE · author_confirmed · 2026-08-24 · also cited as `RULING 115`, `R115`, `R-115`*

(Adopted 2026-08-24, item 8, closing the diagnosis on `JOB02`. Supersedes
nothing.)

**An alarm must be able to tell an EXERCISE from an EVENT. One that cannot will
eventually cry wolf, and the cost is never the false alarm — it is the real one
nobody reads.**

*The rationale stays attached, because a stripped rule reads as guidance.*
`JOB02` recorded that `refresh-meetings-snapshot` failed on two CONSECUTIVE runs
and healed unexamined, and reasoned — correctly, by the rule as it stood — that
two in a row is evidence the cause is ours rather than a host refusing on a
schedule. The watcher raised a **P1 Needs Sean row**.

**Both runs were deliberate drills.** Runs `32543393133` and `32543652154`, five
minutes apart, both `workflow_dispatch`, both carrying
`WTP_INGEST_FORCE_JOB_FAILURE`, and both logging the ingest's own sentence:
*"This failure is FORCED … No vendor failed. No source failed."* Somebody was
testing this very watcher and it worked.

So the alarm performed perfectly and produced a row nobody could act on. **The
Needs Sean queue is precisely where that cost lands**: it is the one channel
that reaches a person, and an item in it that turns out to be nothing teaches
the reader to skim the next one.

Three parts, and the last two are the ones easy to get wrong:

- **Only the test that RAISES a row is narrowed.** The failure RATE still counts
  every run, because the rate is a fact about the workflow and a drill did fail.
- **The number set aside is PRINTED on every run.** A deliberate exclusion that
  reads as a clean result is the silent-trim shape this file names more often
  than any other.
- **An UNKNOWN trigger is not a drill.** Where the kind of run cannot be read,
  the alarm still fires. That direction costs a wasted look; the other loses a
  real failure.

*Why the trigger rather than the forced flag.* The flag lives in the run's
INPUTS, which the run list does not carry, so reading it means a log fetch per
run — forty logs to answer one question. The trigger is already in the list, and
it is the better question anyway: **a watcher exists to catch a job breaking on
its OWN CADENCE**, and a manual dispatch is a person doing something deliberate.
The workflow already refuses the force flag unless the run is a dispatch, so
every drill is a dispatch by construction.

The machinery is `runsOnOwnCadence` in `lib/ops/job-watch.ts`, guarded in
`tests/watch-workflows.test.ts` — including the case that matters more, *a real
scheduled double failure STILL raises a row*, so narrowing the input cannot have
narrowed the detector.

*Adopted 2026-08-24 (the overnight depth hunt, item 8, closing the diagnosis on `JOB02`). Law: `CLAUDE.md`, **Non-negotiables in code**. Supersedes nothing.*

**An alarm must be able to tell an exercise from an event. One that cannot will eventually cry wolf, and the cost is not the false alarm — it is the real one nobody reads.**

A watcher raised a priority-one row saying a scheduled job had failed twice in a row and recovered without anyone finding out why. That is exactly what the watcher is for, and two failures in a row is good evidence the cause is ours rather than the world's.

**Both runs were deliberate tests.** They were five minutes apart, both started by hand rather than on the schedule, both carrying the flag whose only purpose is to make the job fail on purpose — and the job's own log said so in each: *"This failure is FORCED… No vendor failed. No source failed."* Somebody was testing this very watcher, and it worked.

So the alarm did its job perfectly and produced a row nobody could act on. That is the failure this ruling names: **a queue that reaches a person is a scarce thing, and an item in it that turns out to be nothing teaches the reader to skim the next one.**

Three things about the fix, and the second and third are the ones easy to get wrong:

- **Only the test that RAISES a row is narrowed.** The failure RATE still counts every run, because the rate is a fact about the workflow and a drill really did fail.
- **The number set aside is printed on every run.** A deliberate exclusion that reads as a clean result is the same shape as a silent trim, and this project names that failure more often than any other.
- **An unknown trigger is NOT treated as a drill.** Where it cannot be told which kind a run was, the alarm still fires. That is the direction that costs a wasted look; the other direction loses a real failure.

## RULING 131 — a partial source is a first-class result, and completeness is never inferred from `ok: true`

*`R-0131` · ACTIVE · author_confirmed · 2026-08-24 · also cited as `RULING 131`, `R131`, `R-131`*


*Adopted 2026-08-24. Answers **A-004** and **S-002**. Law: `CLAUDE.md`, the
refresh corollary. It EXTENDS it; it narrows nothing.*

**A result says which SCOPE failed, for which divisions, and why. Carry-forward
preserves that scope and no other.**

`ical` fetches two feeds per body. The past feed's failure was caught by an
EMPTY `catch` whose comment read: *this row still produces its upcoming
sittings, and the archive's absence is visible as a jurisdiction with no
concluded meetings.* **That sentence is the render-default failure written down
as a design note** — an outage rendering as a fact about the town.

The chain: archive refuses → adapter reports success → carry-forward preserves
rows only for a source or division that FAILED → every concluded meeting the
previous snapshot held is deleted.

Marking the whole division unreachable would be wrong the other way: the
upcoming feed answered, and carrying its rows forward would resurrect a sitting
the town had just cancelled. So an `ARCHIVE` failure carries back only sittings
that had already concluded — asserted in both directions.

## RULING 146 — a session runs unattended, and nothing it runs may be able to ask it a question

*`R-0146` · AMENDED · author_confirmed · 2026-08-25 · also cited as `RULING 146`, `R146`, `R-146`*


(Adopted 2026-08-25, Sean's standing instruction, made law for every future
session rather than repeated in every brief.)

**Nobody is watching. A question asked is hours lost.**

- A decision that is genuinely Sean's becomes a **Needs Sean row** and the
  session keeps going. It never waits and it never ends its turn to ask.
- **No command may be capable of prompting.** Non-interactive flags everywhere,
  `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0`, `GH_PROMPT=disabled`, stdin closed, every
  long-running command inside a timeout. Five silent minutes is a kill, a row,
  and carry on.
- **Ambiguity resolves against the repo.** The repo is the thing that can be
  checked; a brief is a description of it written earlier.
- **"Ran out of room" is not a blocker.** Neither is a wall, a refusal, or a
  missing input — each is a finding with a row.

*Why this is law and not a header.* It has been the top of every brief for days
and it is a fact about how this project runs, not about one night's work. A rule
that has to be restated every time is a rule that will eventually be left out of
a brief, and the session that reads that brief will stop and wait.

## RULING 150 — a Needs Sean row states its ask as an answerable question, with options

*`R-0150` · ACTIVE · author_confirmed · 2026-08-25 · also cited as `RULING 150`, `R150`, `R-150`*

(Adopted 2026-08-25.)

**A row in that section ends with a QUESTION the author can answer, and the
options he is choosing between. A row that cannot state one is misfiled and is
rerouted to the section that owns the work.**

*The rationale.* Needs Sean is the only channel that reaches a person, and it
stood at 48 open. A row that describes a situation without asking anything
cannot be closed by him — there is nothing to say — so it sits there forever,
and every row like it makes the queue less likely to be read at all. That is the
accumulation RULING 79 was adopted over, arriving through a different door.

- **Not every long row is misfiled.** A row asking a genuine judgement call is
  correct however long it is; what is misfiled is a row asking nobody anything.
- **A rerouted row is never reworded** (RULING 41) and is never closed by the
  reroute. It moves to the section that owns the work and stays open there.
- **An ask is a property of the SENTENCE, not of its punctuation.** Measured on
  adoption: only 5 of 44 rows contained a question mark, and 43 of 44 carried a
  real ask. A mechanical sweep would have rerouted 39 rows that genuinely need
  him.

prose neither author wrote would be composition.*


(Adopted 2026-08-25.)

**A row in that section ends with a QUESTION Sean can answer, and the options he
is choosing between. A row that cannot state one is misfiled and is rerouted to
the section that owns the work.**

*The rationale.* Needs Sean is the only channel that reaches a person, and it
stood at 48 open. A row that describes a situation without asking anything
cannot be closed by him — there is nothing to say — so it sits there forever,
and every row like it makes the queue less likely to be read at all. That is the
accumulation RULING 79 was adopted over, arriving through a different door.

- **Not every long row is misfiled.** A row asking a genuine judgement call is
  correct however long it is; what is misfiled is a row asking nobody anything.
- **A rerouted row is never reworded** (RULING 41) and is never closed by the
  reroute. It moves to the section that owns the work and stays open there.

</details>

## RULING 208 — an access escalation is a parallel lane, never a stop

*`R-0208` · ACTIVE · author_explicit · 2026-08-29 · also cited as `RULING 208`, `R208`, `R-208`*

- **amends** → `R-0146`
  - what changed: what a Needs Sean row leaves running. RULING 146 keeps the SESSION going past the row; this extends that to the OBLIGATION the row is about — an access escalation never closes, pauses or satisfies the underlying acquisition obligation — and it gives the row a required content shape, because a row that names no provider, mechanism, scope or unlocked capability cannot be acted on by the author it was written for
  - what survives, in force: RULING 146 entire: nobody is watching, a question asked is hours lost, a decision genuinely the author's becomes a row and the session keeps going, no command may be capable of prompting, ambiguity resolves against the repo, and 'ran out of room' is not a blocker
- **extends** → `R-0190`
- **sets** `escalation.access_request` = `parallel-never-blocking`

**An access escalation is a PARALLEL LANE. It never stops the record
obligation, and it never stops unrelated work.**

Where an API token, vendor account, public-data key, authorized service account,
bulk export, government feed, quota increase or documented gated route would
MATERIALLY improve retrieval, say so immediately and precisely — and keep
working every other executable path while the answer is outstanding.

    API_KEY_WOULD_HELP   is not   BLOCKED
    NEEDS SEAN           is not   STOP

RULING 146 says the SESSION keeps going past a row. This says the same of the
thing the row is about: **opening an access escalation never closes, pauses or
satisfies the underlying acquisition obligation**, and the detective,
acquisition, extraction, reconciliation and reader streams all continue against
every other representation while it is open. The correct simultaneous state is
*escalation open* AND *acquisition still running*.

**The escalation carries its own content, or it is not one.** Name the provider
and the exact access mechanism; the record class it would improve; the
capability it appears to expose and whether documentation confirms it; whether
it is public, paid, government-sponsored or partner-only; the signup, request or
contact path if known; the minimum scopes needed; what the system continues to
do WITHOUT it; and what completeness or reliability it would unlock. A row
reading only "an API key would help" is not an escalation.

**Never ask the author to paste a secret into chat, a prompt, a tracker row, a
commit, a fixture or a log.** A credential once obtained travels the
repository's governed secret path.

**The narrow exception is still not absence.** Where every machine-accessible
public path for that exact record has genuinely been worked and only a human or
account action remains, the state is **PUBLIC RECORD STILL OWED — HUMAN/ACCOUNT
ACCESS REQUIRED**, which is RULING 205's third close and not a fourth one.
**One blocked record never freezes the rest of the civic hunt.**

## RULING 227 — escalation without reconciliation is prohibited

*`R-0227` · ACTIVE · author_explicit · 2026-08-31 · also cited as `RULING 227`, `R227`, `R-227`*

- **extends** → `R-0208`
- **related_to** → `R-0221`
- **related_to** → `R-0146`
- **related_to** → `R-0055`
- **sets** `escalation.entry_requirement` = `machine-predicate-or-explicit-not-verifiable-with-card`
- **sets** `escalation.reconciliation_cadence` = `rechecked-every-generation-auto-resolves`

**A row may not enter NEEDS_SEAN without either (a) a machine-verifiable
predicate that is rechecked on EVERY tracker generation and AUTO-RESOLVES the
row when the predicate goes false, or (b) an explicit NOT_MACHINE_VERIFIABLE
marking carrying a decision card. Escalation without reconciliation is
prohibited.**

## The measured failure

The queue held 72 Needs-Sean rows and no opened dates. Three of them were
presented to the author as current blockers in a session close-out:

```
  NH272  the read-only DB secret EXISTS; production integrity performs a
         live 24/24 migration read
  NH281  "stuck since 7/13/2025" — two application-bearing releases had
         published and been observed HELD
  NH300  a 7/7 LIVE POSTGRES proof was on disk when the row was presented
         as blocked on obtaining one
```

All three had been true when written. None was true when shown. **The queue had
no mechanism capable of noticing**, so the rows aged into falsehood and were
then reported to the author as the current state of his own project.

## Why the fix is a predicate and not a review cadence

A review cadence puts the burden on a session to re-check 72 rows, which is
exactly the work that did not happen for months. A predicate puts the burden on
the GENERATOR, which runs every time. The row states the condition that makes
it blocked, in a form a machine can evaluate:

```
  NEEDS_SEAN  requires  BLOCKED_WHILE: <predicate>
                        rechecked on every generation
                        false -> the row AUTO-RESOLVES, with the evidence
```

A row that cannot state such a predicate is not thereby exempt — it is marked
NOT_MACHINE_VERIFIABLE, explicitly, and carries a decision card. The marking is
the point: it makes the un-checkable rows a visible, countable set rather than
the invisible default.

## The decision card, and what it is for

A NEEDS_SEAN row's whole purpose is to get a decision made. A row that names a
problem without stating the options makes the author do the analysis before he
can do the deciding, which is why the queue grew. Every card carries: what is
needed; the options; the consequence of each; and the row's AGE — because an
old decision and a new one are different decisions, and the author cannot see
which he is looking at without the date.

## This does not weaken RULING 208 or RULING 221

RULING 208 stands entire: *NEEDS SEAN never closes, pauses or satisfies the
obligation the row is about*, and one blocked record never freezes the rest of
the hunt. RULING 221 stands entire: NEEDS_OWNER is TERMINAL within a session's
denominator and is never counted as open executable work. This rule governs
only whether a row may ENTER the queue, and what must happen to it while it
sits there.

## An agent does not know today's date, and a date not read from the system clock is a fabrication.

*`R-C-repo-layout-an-agent-does-not-know-today-s-date-and-a-date-not-r` · ACTIVE · author_explicit · date UNKNOWN — the source carried no stamp (RULING 107)*

**An agent does not know today's date, and a date not read from the system clock is a fabrication.** Every stamp entering any document — a tracker Note, a `state.md` section, an `Adopted` line in this file, a provenance field — comes from `pnpm stamp`, which prints today in `America/Phoenix` (a UTC read after 5pm local is a day ahead, and that is the same bug wearing a smaller hat). A plausible date is not a date; it is the same failure as a generated candidate position — a confident claim with nothing behind it — and it is worse here, because it misdates the rule every later decision was supposedly made under. Guarded at authorship by the pre-commit hook and in the suite by `tests/doc-dates.test.ts`; `pnpm verify-stamps` audits this file's `Adopted` stamps against the git history that would have to be true for them, and writes `docs/stamp-audit.md` for the author to rule on. Nothing corrects a stamp automatically — an agent that repaired a date would be doing the thing that caused the defect.

## Priority is three levels, ranked inside a section and never across them

*`R-C-repo-layout-priority-is-three-levels-ranked-inside-a-section-and` · ACTIVE · author_explicit · date UNKNOWN — the source carried no stamp (RULING 107)*

**Priority is three levels, ranked inside a section and never across them** (RULING 29): P1 broken or blocking, P2 needed before the section is done, P3 wanted but not needed. Five P1 rows maximum per section (RULING 30) — a section over the cap is REPORTED as stopped, and **the cap is never satisfied by demotion**. Every row has a home in `docs/tracker-sections.json` and there is no holding section (RULING 32). **Gaps are not tracker rows** (RULING 33): a gap is a measurement of coverage and lives in `docs/gap-ledger.md`, which is generated and therefore current; the tracker holds the decision to hunt a place, and the ledger holds which of that place's bodies are still dark.

## Task status lives in the TWO TRACKER STORES, and the tracker is a queue that empties.

*`R-C-repo-layout-task-status-lives-in-the-two-tracker-stores-and-the` · ACTIVE · author_explicit · 2026-08-20*

- **derived_from** → `R-0035`

**Task status lives in the TWO TRACKER STORES, and the tracker is a queue that empties.** (Rewritten 2026-08-20, Prompt E items 6 and 13; RULING 35.) `docs/tracker-working.csv` holds every OPEN row and `docs/tracker-resolved.csv` holds every finished one. A finished row LEAVES the working view and lands in the resolved store, so the number the author looks at is what is left rather than everything that has ever existed. **Nothing is ever deleted**; the resolved store is permanent and is the record of what was decided and when. `docs/tracker.xlsx` is the workbook he edits by hand — Working, Resolved, and a tab explaining both. `docs/tracker.md` and `docs/log.md` are generated views and are never hand-edited. `docs/tracker.csv` is the FROZEN pre-rebuild snapshot: read for history, never written again, digest-pinned in `tests/tracker-stores.test.ts`.

Update the row for any item you work on, in the same commit as the work, through `corepack pnpm tracker:move` — nothing else writes the stores. **A status change edits the existing row. It never appends a second row with the same ID** — a tracker with two rows per ID cannot be read by anything, and it silently breaks every lookup by ID. M02 and M04 each carried a duplicate pair for a day before anyone noticed. Nothing is resolved without evidence: the branch name, and which of `test` / `lint` / `build` passed. A commit SHA cannot be used — it does not exist inside the commit that would name it. An agent grading its own homework drifts optimistic; this tracker only earns its keep if it tells the truth.
